items.title: George "Tex" Stephens Interview, 1995-08-29
items.q: he had brought in Roy Brown, then he had a combination with Roy Brown... I think Okie Doke and myself, we all went, we were just hanging out

ctx.x: What about some of the, I was talking about the ancillary clubs, and like, you know, like Foster's? How was Foster's?

George Foster was two blocks from the Doudrop, still right there on LaSalle Street. George Foster had the little downtown club, I mean the uptown club, and he wasn't the promoter that Frank Pena was. He was the guy who fell in line. But he started bringing in, like, well he had brought in Roy Brown, then he had a combination with Roy Brown, and went on the Irish with the first Battle of the Blues that I could recall in the city of New Orleans. That went on for around about maybe five hours between the two of…
Straight A, not straight A's. Something about Aces.

items.title: George "Tex" Stephens Interview, 1996-01-10
items.q: Roy Brown, like I said, really started this thing in New Orleans, even before Fats Domino, in a sense, because he had this good rock and tonight thing

ctx.x: Well, when you hear that terminology, what does that mean? You heard it in the mid-fifties. You first heard it.

Well, when I first heard it, I looked at it and said, rock and roll. Well, you see, Roy Brown, like I said, really started this thing in New Orleans, even before Fats Domino, in a sense, because he had this good rock and tonight thing, and he had this band with Bob Bob Ockton. Bob Ockton was an ordinary, but he was a drummer. He died a couple of years back, you know, and incidentally, some of his relatives say, no, I'm no real business right now. I talk to him every now and then. So, when you're good rocking…

Well, well, did you, I know you probably did, and there's a whole article in the Jazz Archivist. Yeah. And we're talking about New Orleans in the 60s, and they're talking about, a lot of it about the modern jazz scene. Did you follow the pop, the bebop scene in New Orleans?
